insight.title: Why the stars stay in place
insight.subtitle: Understanding the invisible architecture of the night sky

sections.text: Look up on a clear night and everything seems perfectly still. We see the moon and distant stars as fixed points in a vast, empty room. But space is not a void. It is a soft, invisible fabric that stretches and curves around every planet, sun, and person, holding the entire universe in a quiet, steady embrace.

Think of a heavy glass marble resting on a sheet of dark silk. The weight creates a gentle dip, drawing everything nearby toward the center. This is how gravity works. Large worlds curve the space around them, guiding moons and light along elegant, invisible paths. Nothing is falling; everything is simply following the beautiful geometry of the dark.

This invisible architecture keeps our feet on the grass and our air from drifting away. It is the silent rhythm that governs the tides and the morning sun. We are not just floating in a vacuum; we are cradled by the very shape of the universe. Even in the stillness, we are part of a grand, moving design.

news.title: New research initiative aims to predict and prevent diseases before they start
news.description: What if doctors could tell you a disease was coming years before you felt a single symptom-and stop it in its tracks? That is the goal of a sweeping new research initiative launched by the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in collaboration with the Uniformed Services University of the Health Sciences (USU) and the Henry M. Jackson Foundation for the Advancement of Military Medicine (HJF).

news.title: Brain scans of Buddhist monks reveal how different meditation styles alter consciousness
news.description: By measuring the magnetic fields of the brain, researchers found that different contemplative practices uniquely change how our minds balance strict order and total chaos. These shifts make neural activity more adaptable and less predictable over time.

news.title: A bold new plan could finally cure type 1 diabetes
news.description: Researchers are developing a two-part therapy for type 1 diabetes: lab-made insulin-producing cells paired with custom-engineered immune cells that protect them. The goal is to stop the immune system from destroying transplanted cells — without using immunosuppressive drugs. Backed by $1 million in funding, the team hopes to create a ready-to-use treatment that could work even for people who have had diabetes for years. The approach could transform how the disease is treated.
